subject: chemistry
title: Bond enthalpies
key_idea: Breaking bonds takes in energy and making bonds gives out energy. **Mean bond enthalpies** let you estimate ΔH for a reaction of gases as the energy to break the bonds in the reactants minus the energy released making the bonds in the products. The answer is approximate.

blocks.text: All chemical reactions break some bonds and make others. The balance between the two decides whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.

items.meaning: The enthalpy change when 1 mol of a particular bond is broken in gaseous molecules. It is always positive.
The average enthalpy change to break 1 mol of a bond, taken over a range of different molecules containing that bond.

items: Breaking bonds is endothermic. Energy is taken in to pull the atoms apart.
Making bonds is exothermic. The same amount of energy is given out when the bond forms.
Exothermic reaction: more energy is released making the new bonds than is needed to break the old ones.
Endothermic reaction: more energy is needed to break the old bonds than is released making the new ones.
Bond enthalpies are for gases, because the molecules must be separate for the bond to be broken without other forces.
Bond breaking is endothermic. Bond making is exothermic.
Bond enthalpy values are positive and refer to gaseous molecules.
The overall sign of ΔH depends on which is bigger.

sections.heading: Calculating ΔH from mean bond enthalpies

blocks.text: Add up the bonds broken and the bonds made, using the balanced equation. Multiply each bond enthalpy by how many of that bond there are.

blocks.label: Enthalpy change from bond enthalpies
where: Σ(bonds broken) = total bond enthalpy of the reactants, in kJ mol⁻¹
Σ(bonds made) = total bond enthalpy of the products, in kJ mol⁻¹

items.text: Show the full structure of each molecule, so that no bond is missed.
H₂ + Cl₂ breaks one H–H (436) and one Cl–Cl (243): 679 kJ mol⁻¹.
2HCl makes two H–Cl bonds (432 each): 864 kJ mol⁻¹.
ΔH = 679 − 864 = −185 kJ mol⁻¹. It is exothermic.

diagram.question: H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g). Bond enthalpies: H–H 436, Cl–Cl **{c}**, H–Cl **{h}** kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate ΔH.

items: If ΔH is given and one bond enthalpy is missing, write the equation ΔH = broken − made with the unknown in it, then solve.
Check the sign of your answer against what you expect: a reaction that releases heat must give a negative ΔH.
ΔH = bonds broken − bonds made.
Count every bond, using the number shown in the balanced equation.
A negative answer means exothermic; a positive answer means endothermic.

sections.heading: Why bond enthalpy values are only approximate

blocks.text: Values from mean bond enthalpies differ from values found using Hess's law, which uses the real substances.

items: A mean value is an average over many molecules. The actual bond enthalpy in a particular molecule may be different.
For example, the C–H bond has a different enthalpy in methane than in ethane, so the mean is not exact for either.
The calculation assumes every substance is a gas. In liquid or solid substances, there are also attractions between molecules, which are ignored.
Some bond energies are exact. The bond in a diatomic molecule such as H₂ or Cl₂ occurs in only one molecule, so it has one definite value.
Hess's law uses measured values for the actual compounds, so it gives more reliable results.
Mean values are averages, so the answer is only an estimate.
Exact values exist for bonds in diatomic molecules.
Hess's law with formation or combustion data is more accurate.

items: Average bond enthalpy is the breaking of 1 mol of bonds in gaseous molecules. A formal definition is not required.
Understand that an actual bond enthalpy may differ from the average value.
